title: In which forms should I think of you?
hookLine: Arjuna believes Krishna is everything, then asks where to look; why Hindus pray before a murti
last: THE SOURCE — I AM THE ORIGIN.

cards: Picture the chariot, parked between two armies.

For nine chapters, Krishna, Arjuna's friend and driver, has been telling him what's real: the self in every heart, the one all beings rest in, and yesterday, the source of everything, even the gods. Arjuna believes it.
He says so, out loud. And then this warrior, the finest archer of his age, admits he doesn't know where to aim. You're everything, he says, and I believe it.
But how do I think of you? In which things, which forms?

teach.b: Verse twelve is Arjuna's confession of faith. You are the highest Brahman, the highest home, the eternal divine person, the first god, unborn, all-pervading. The sages say so, he adds: Narada, Asita and Devala, Vyasa.
And now you say it yourself.

teach.h: I ACCEPT IT ALL AS TRUE.
teach.b: Verse fourteen: I accept everything you've told me as true. Verse fifteen: only you know yourself, by yourself, god of gods, lord of the world.
Then verse sixteen: tell me your divine glories, vibhutis, the powers by which you fill all these worlds. And verse seventeen: how shall I know you, master of yoga?

teach.h: IN WHICH FORMS SHOULD I THINK OF YOU?
teach.b: In which things, in which forms, should I think of you? Verse eighteen: tell me again, in detail; your words are nectar, and I never tire of them. It's a humble question, and a deeply Hindu one.
Hindus hold that God is infinite and everywhere.
And yet in most Hindu homes there's a shrine with a murti, an image of Krishna, Ganesha or the Goddess, a lamp and a flower in front of it. That isn't a contradiction.
Many Hindus believe God, lovingly invited, is truly present in the murti, but never only there.

teach.h: THE INFINITE, MET THROUGH A FORM.
teach.b: A person needs somewhere to put their eyes and their love, and many teachers read Arjuna's question in just this way: the infinite, met through a form. Tomorrow, Krishna's answer. Today, the question.

how: Most Hindu homes keep a murti or picture of God at a shrine; many Hindus explain it as Arjuna's question suggests: God is everywhere, and the image is where you place your eyes and your love.

o: a plea for handles to think of God by
a request to call off the coming war
a doubt that Krishna is truly divine

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: in which things should I think of you?

s: Arjuna doubts what Krishna has said
verse 14: I accept everything you've told me as true.
Arjuna asks for specific things to think of Krishna in
verse 17: in which things, which forms, should I think of you?
verse 18: tell me again, in detail; I never tire of your words.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you believe Krishna is the source of everything. what do you ask next?
o: in which things should I think of you?
games.why: he asks for handles: in which things, which forms, should I think of you? chapter ten's list is the answer, and it's the same reason a Hindu home keeps a murti.

practice: If there's a murti, a picture of God or a sacred image near you, sit facing it; if not, choose one simple thing in front of you, a candle, a plant, a patch of sky.

Look at it slowly and let it be your handle, the way Arjuna asked for one. If you pray, greet God in it with folded hands, as many Hindus do each morning. If not, let it stand for something bigger than you.

wordCard.voice: Arjuna asks. After believing it all, he asks: in which forms should I think of you? Give me something to hold.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vibhuti, divine glory, manifestation of power; also the sacred ash many Hindus wear.

carryVoice: Your line: the infinite, met through forms. That's what the murti on the shelf is for. That's day one hundred ninety-four.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 10.16–10.18 (in which things should I think of you?)
